html:
Introduction

Have you ever seen a piece of food that looks remarkably similar to chicken and wondered whether it could actually be made from plant protein?

Modern food science has made it possible to transform plant proteins such as soy and wheat gluten into products with fibrous, layered, and meat-like textures. These meat analogues are intentionally designed to resemble foods such as chicken strips, nuggets and other meat products.

At the same time, concerns about meat adulteration and species substitution are legitimate food-authenticity issues. However, these two concepts should not be confused. A plant-based chicken analogue is deliberately manufactured as a meat alternative, whereas adulterated meat involves the undeclared substitution or addition of another substance or species.

So, can plant protein really be made to look and feel like chicken? Yes. But can you prove that a piece of chicken is fake simply because it looks fibrous or pulls apart in a certain way? No.

Understanding how plant proteins are processed—and how food authenticity is actually tested—helps separate genuine food science from misleading claims based on appearance alone.

Have you ever seen a piece of food that looks remarkably similar to chicken and wondered whether it could actually be made from plant protein?

Modern food-processing technology can transform plant proteins such as soy protein and wheat gluten into highly structured, fibrous materials that resemble the texture of meat. This is a genuine food-science technology and is widely used to manufacture plant-based meat analogues designed to resemble products such as chicken strips, nuggets, and other meat products.

But does this mean that ordinary chicken can be secretly replaced with soy protein and wheat gluten?

Not necessarily.

It is important to distinguish between legitimate food technology and food adulteration or substitution.

How Can Plant Protein Become Meat-Like?

Proteins from plants do not naturally have the same fibrous structure as skeletal muscle. However, controlled food-processing techniques can dramatically change their physical structure.

One important method is high-moisture extrusion. During this process, plant proteins are mixed with water and exposed to controlled heat, pressure, and mechanical shear.

These thermo-mechanical conditions cause the proteins to unfold, interact, and reorganize into aligned structures.

Soy protein can contribute substantially to the protein matrix, while wheat gluten can provide important elastic and extensible properties. Under suitable processing conditions, the interaction between these proteins can produce a fibrous, layered structure that resembles the texture of meat.

This is why some plant-based meat products can appear surprisingly similar to chicken when they are cut, pulled, or cooked.

The important point is that similar texture does not necessarily mean identical composition.

Can Plant Proteins Be Used to Make Chicken-Like Products?

Yes.

Food scientists can deliberately engineer plant proteins to reproduce some of the physical characteristics of meat, including:

* Fibrous texture
* Elasticity
* Layering
* Moisture retention
* Chewiness
* Appearance

Such products are known as meat analogues or meat alternatives.

They are manufactured intentionally using food-processing technology and should not automatically be confused with adulterated meat.

A plant-based chicken analogue may look and behave remarkably like chicken while containing no animal muscle tissue at all.

But What About Meat Adulteration?

Meat adulteration and species substitution are genuine food-authenticity and food-safety concerns.

Food products can potentially be mislabelled or substituted for financial gain. For example, a higher-value meat may be replaced or mixed with a lower-value meat, meat from an undeclared species, or other undeclared ingredients.

The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has recognized meat adulteration and substitution as important food-authenticity concerns. Detection can become more difficult when meat has been highly processed, minced, or otherwise comminuted because processing can remove or obscure characteristics that would otherwise help identify the original material.

However, this does not mean that ordinary chicken pieces are routinely being replaced with soy protein and wheat gluten.

That conclusion cannot be made simply by looking at a piece of chicken.

Can You Identify Fake Chicken by Pulling It Apart?

No.

This is one of the most important points.

Genuine chicken is composed of skeletal muscle fibres, so naturally cooked chicken can have a fibrous, stringy, or layered appearance.

Plant-based meat analogues can also be engineered to produce fibrous structures.

Therefore, fibrous texture alone cannot prove that meat is fake or adulterated.

Similarly, colour, appearance, chewiness, or the way a piece of meat separates when pulled apart cannot reliably establish whether it contains chicken, another animal species, soy protei,n or another ingredient.

How Can Food Composition Actually Be Confirmed?

When there is a genuine concern about food authenticity, appropriate laboratory testing is required.

Depending on the question being investigated, laboratories can use analytical techniques designed to identify:

* Animal species
* Plant-derived proteins
* Specific ingredients
* DNA from animal species
* Undeclared components

Therefore, a viral video showing someone pulling apart a piece of meat cannot, by itself, establish that the product is adulterated.

Visual appearance is not a laboratory test.

The Science Behind the Viral Confusion

The confusion arises because two completely different situations can produce similar-looking fibrous structures.

In one situation, food scientists intentionally use controlled processing to transform soy protein and wheat gluten into a meat-like structure.

In another situation, genuine animal muscle naturally contains organized protein fibres that give meat its characteristic texture.

Both can therefore appear fibrous.

This is why texture alone cannot be used as proof of food fraud.

Conclusion

Yes, modern food science can transform plant proteins such as soy protein and wheat gluten into highly structured, fibrous materials capable of resembling chicken in texture.

Yes, meat adulteration and species substitution are real food-authenticity concerns.

But a fibrous or stringy piece of chicken does not prove that it is fake, and there is no scientific basis for concluding that ordinary chicken has been replaced with plant protein simply because it resembles a meat analogue.

If the composition of a food product needs to be established, appropriate laboratory testing—not visual inspection—is required.

Similar appearance does not necessarily mean similar composition.

Scientific Reference

1. Peng Y, Zhao D, Li M, Wen X, Ni Y. The Interactions of Soy Protein and Wheat Gluten for the Development of Meat-like Fibrous Structure. Molecules. 2023;28(21):7431.
DOI: 10.3390/molecules28217431.

Food-Safety Reference

Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI). Guidance Note: Safety and Quality of Meat and Poultry. FSSAI discusses adulteration/substitution of meat for financial gain, including the use of lower-value meat and unknown species, and notes the increased difficulty of detecting adulteration in processed/comminuted meat products.
